paras: The attempted lynching of Thomas Wayne took place at Hinton, West Virginia, on August 16, 1910, when a crowd of 1,000 or more tried to seize a Black prisoner charged with assaulting and killing Mrs. John Alliff near Quinnimont. The sheriff slipped away with him after dark while the governor sent militia, and the Advocate of Charleston, a Black weekly, condemned the mob's reported cry that he was "only a nigger."

Reports from Charleston said that on Sunday night, August 14, John Alliff, a Chesapeake and Ohio brakeman, was beaten and robbed on the tracks near Quinnimont and his bride of three weeks assaulted and killed. While posses with bloodhounds searched the mountains, Officer C. D. Duke and two others arrested Wayne, a power-house worker whom Alliff thought resembled his attacker. The Bluefield Evening Leader reported that a shirt with stained sleeves was found in his cabin; he said the stains were rust.

Duke brought the prisoner to the Summers County jail at Hinton about 2 p.m., and crowds gathered until, in the Fairmont West Virginian's words, "Hinton was a mob ridden city." Officials agreed with the mob's leaders to move him to the station, but the special train's engine and those at the round house had been disabled. According to an Omaha Daily Bee dispatch, the mob guarded the car from 5 until 9 o'clock while the town's electric wires were cut.

Brought to the car to identify the prisoner, Alliff would not look at him; the Fairmont paper thought he refused to prevent a lynching, and the Falmouth Outlook said he pleaded with the mob. The crowd cried "lynch him, he's only a nigger anyway" and tried to rush the car, but armed guards held it, and ten or twelve ringleaders were jailed.

After dark Sheriff Wiseman and two deputies took the prisoner down the track toward Avis while the mob's leaders ran toward the jail. They waded and swam two rivers and hid the manacled man under hay in a wagon for a forty-mile drive, reaching Princeton on the morning of August 17. Three or four militia companies reached Hinton, which was put under martial rule.

Troops under General E. L. Boggs moved the prisoner from Welch to the Huntington jail on August 18, and Wiseman denied reports of a confession. On August 23 Huntington officials said he had confessed and that Alliff had identified him; he was later reported picked from a line of a dozen men. A special grand jury was announced but not called, and the case went over to the October term; no report of an indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The Fairmont West Virginian said Detective Duke would answer to the governor for bringing the prisoner to Hinton on the same train as the dead woman's body. Late in August mobs stormed the Huntington jail on two nights to lynch Wayne and another prisoner, Charles Clayburne, and on September 3 both were moved to the Moundsville penitentiary.

White papers framed the story as a mob outwitted, with headlines such as "Judge Lynch Robbed" in the Ottumwa Tri-Weekly Courier and "Negro in Hay Wagon Saved from the Mob" in the Washington Times. The wires could not agree on his name, calling him John Wayne, James Dawson, John Howard or Thomas Raymond. The Fairmont West Virginian headlined him a "brute" while praising the officers, and its later editorials warned against mob punishment of a possibly innocent man.

The only Black-press treatment of Hinton found is the Advocate's editorial of August 25, "Only a Nigger," which reported the mob's answer to pleas for law: "he is only a nigger, let us have him." The editorial argued that lynching Black people endangered white citizens too. The Twin City Star later reprinted the wire on the Huntington jail riots naming Wayne.

The Bluefield Evening Leader placed the escape on "Monday night" and the Richmond Virginian said the prisoner was returned to the Hinton jail, against the other reports. Estimates of the crowd ran from 1,000 to 1,500. The confession came only from Huntington officials; Wiseman had denied one, and a same-day Clarksburg report said Alliff had not yet viewed the prisoner.

No one was killed: the mob of 1,000 to 1,500 tried to take the prisoner, accused of murder, but the sheriff got him to Princeton alive [A9, A11, A26]; it was an attempted lynching.

accounts.gist: Three companies of militia at Hinton to prevent the lynching of 'John Wayne'; he escaped from a mob of 1,000; Ailliss too ill to identify him; martial rule.

accounts.gist: The sheriff drove the manacled prisoner hidden under hay forty miles to Princeton after wading and swimming two rivers; the accused protested innocence and said the stains were rust.

accounts.label: Huntington officials
accounts.gist: On August 23 Wayne confessed to Sheriff Kinchlee and Prosecuting Attorney Love and was identified by Alliff.

accounts.label: Black editorial (Advocate)
accounts.gist: The mob answered pleas for the law with 'he is only a nigger, let us have him'; lynching Black men endangers whites too.

framing.detail: Wire headlines framed it as a lynching thwarted: 'Judge Lynch Robbed', 'Negro in Hay Wagon Saved from the Mob', 'Troops Guard Negro'.
Fairmont West Virginian called the accused a 'brute' and 'murderer and ravisher' in headlines while praising officers and warning against lynching an innocent man.
Seattle Star's 'Bride's Head Cut Off' repeated the posse leaders' promise to lynch, days after the arrest.
Advocate editorial 'Only a Nigger' turned the mob's cry against it and condemned mob law.
